title: Insect flight: wing number, wing form, and steering
question: Could you redesign an insect's flight apparatus - and if you added wings, would it fly better?
short_answer: The experiment has been done since 1978 and the answer is no, for two independent reasons that the literature separates cleanly: the second pair of wings has almost no engine, and the organ you spent to get it was a rate gyroscope. Neither of those is a general law about four wings - dragonflies have had four independently controlled wings for 300 million years - and the page is organised around what makes the dipteran case different.

scales.label: Molecular · cis-regulatory
scales.blurb: Change non-coding DNA and leave every protein intact. This is the layer at which a Hox gene actually acts - Ubx does not build a haltere, it re-reads the wing's own enhancers - and it is the layer at which evolution has repeatedly changed appendage identity without changing the appendage toolkit.

scales.label: Gene · selectors and identity
scales.blurb: Delete or force the selector proteins themselves. The phenotypes here are the strongest and the oldest in the literature; Lewis's four-winged fly is one of them. They are also the ones that transform the SKIN of a segment and leave its muscle behind, which is the whole problem with the four-winged design.

scales.label: Network · wing specification
scales.blurb: The signalling circuit that decides there will be a wing at all, and how big: Wingless, Notch/Serrate/Delta, Dpp and the Vestigial-Scalloped selector complex. Turning these knobs gives you more wing or less wing, rarely a different KIND of wing.

scales.label: Pattern · venation and blade
scales.blurb: What the wing membrane is actually made of. Veins carry the haemolymph, the tracheae and the campaniform sensilla, and they set the blade's bending stiffness, so a venation change is a structural change and a sensory change at the same time.

scales.label: Actuator · muscle and hinge
scales.blurb: The engine and the gearbox. A wing is useless without the indirect flight muscle that drives the thorax and the hinge sclerites that convert thoracic oscillation into a stroke. This scale is where the four-winged fly fails, and almost nobody asking for a second pair of wings is thinking about it.

scales.label: Sensor · haltere and campaniform system
scales.blurb: The haltere is the hindwing, reduced to a club and rebuilt as a rate gyroscope. Everything that converts a hindwing into a wing deletes it. This scale exists on the page because the obvious design intuition - more wings, better flight - ignores the organ it is proposing to spend.

scales.label: Neural · steering and control
scales.blurb: The loop that closes between sensor and actuator, in under a wingbeat. It is also the layer at which insect flight has already been redesigned by engineers, by implanting stimulators rather than by changing any gene.

scales.label: Organism · plasticity and morph
scales.blurb: Several insects already switch their own wings on and off within a single genome, on an environmental cue. If you want a wing-number change that is reversible and non-lethal, this is the only scale where nature has already solved it.

scales.label: Comparative · other orders
scales.blurb: Four independently controlled wings (Odonata), coupled fore- and hindwings (Lepidoptera), halteres on the WRONG segment (Strepsiptera), and thousands of independent losses of flight. These are the experiments evolution has already run.

NOT against the title: a title routinely names the STARTING condition ('a segment that has no wing'), and matching it tagged six routes with the opposite of their outcome. The order matters - first match wins. Every route also carries a precomputed `outcome` field holding the result of this same matching, checked by hand route by route; if a renderer's own matching disagrees with that field, the field is right and the renderer is wrong.

routes.title: Disable the Ubx-bound enhancers that build a haltere, leaving Ubx protein intact
routes.intervention: Delete or mutate the Ubx-occupied regulatory elements at haltere-specific targets identified by genome-wide occupancy, one target at a time, rather than removing Ubx itself.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A PARTIAL wing-ward transformation of the haltere, target by target, rather than the whole-appendage switch a Ubx null gives. Which traits move depends on which target you hit: Ubx acts on genes at several levels of the wing-patterning hierarchy at once, so no single enhancer carries the whole identity.
routes.mechanism: Ubx is a transcription factor; the haltere is what its targets build. Occupancy maps give the candidate elements, and Ubx's target set CHANGES between stages of haltere morphogenesis, so the same element deleted at a different time is a different experiment.
routes.reversibility: Not reversible in the animal: a germline sequence change. Reversible at the design stage, because each element is independent of the others.
routes.lethality_risk: Low. Ubx protein is untouched, so the segmental and abdominal functions that make a Ubx null lethal are intact.
routes.difficulty: High. The occupancy maps give hundreds of candidates and no map says which are REQUIRED; each one is its own allele.

evidence.cite: Slattery M et al. 2011, PLoS One 6:e14686, 'Genome-wide tissue-specific occupancy of the Hox protein Ultrabithorax and Hox cofactor Homothorax in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: Genome-wide, tissue-specific occupancy of Ubx and its cofactor Homothorax in Drosophila, motivated explicitly by the question of 'what target genes Ubx regulates to generate these adult structures'.

evidence.cite: Pavlopoulos A et al. 2011, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 108:2855-60, 'Hox gene Ultrabithorax regulates distinct sets of target genes at successive stages of Drosophila haltere morphogenesis'
evidence.finding: Ubx 'regulates distinct sets of target genes at successive stages of Drosophila haltere morphogenesis' - so the target list is a function of developmental time, not a fixed set.

evidence.cite: Weatherbee SD et al. 1998, Genes Dev 12:1474-82, 'Ultrabithorax regulates genes at several levels of the wing-patterning hierarchy to shape the development of the Drosophila haltere'
evidence.finding: Ubx 'regulates genes at several levels of the wing-patterning hierarchy'; it represses Wingless and a subset of Wg- and Dpp-activated genes such as spalt-related.

routes.title: Titrate Ubx dose rather than removing it, and ask for an intermediate appendage
routes.intervention: Reduce Ubx protein in the T3 pouch in graded steps - by allelic series, RNAi titration or degron - instead of removing it.
routes.predicted_phenotype: AN INTERMEDIATE APPENDAGE, if the decision is a dial. Wing-like traits appear once Ubx falls to about 39% of its endogenous level, and the approach to that point is the question: a graded appendage or a switch. Our own model (study 1) fits the graded reading and, calibrated on the Ubx arm alone, predicts the independently measured Antp threshold to within 4.0%; the switch-like variant misses it by 39.2%. (An earlier, stale copy of that study reported the gap as a factor of 40; re-running its own code showed the switch-like variant passes the same controls, which makes this a fair comparison and a smaller one.) The sharper test needs no model at all: the two published thresholds sit on OPPOSITE branches of the switch, so their ordering tests hysteresis directly, and under both protein-ratio measurements the ordering is the one a hysteretic switch forbids - under the GFP ratio the two doses are within 4% of each other, i.e. effectively a single threshold.
routes.mechanism: Hox dose, not Hox presence, sets appendage identity. The wing selector Vestigial-Scalloped is repressed by Ubx, and the decision is where that repression crosses the selector's own threshold.
routes.reversibility: Fully reversible if done with a degron or inducible RNAi; this is the most reversible route on the page at the gene scale.
routes.lethality_risk: Low if restricted to the T3 disc.
routes.difficulty: Moderate. The reagents exist; the hard part is measuring the dose rather than assuming it.

evidence.cite: Paul R et al. 2021, Nat Commun 12:2892, 'Hox dosage contributes to flight appendage morphology in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: Full text read (PMC8129201, fetched this session). 'characteristic wing-like phenotypic traits (including veins, hairs organization, and flattening) eventually appeared when the level decreased to 39% of endogenous Ubx'; the paper gives that as 2.5 times lower than endogenous Ubx. And, decisively for study 1's model comparison: 'In both cases, intermediate levels led to intermediary phenotypes' - which is the graded reading, observed directly, independently of any model.

routes.title: Change organ SIZE without changing organ identity, through the Ubx-dally-Dpp axis
routes.intervention: Restore Dpp transcription and mobility in the haltere pouch by de-repressing dally and lowering thickveins, without touching Ubx's identity targets.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A BIGGER haltere that is still a haltere. The haltere ends larval life with roughly fivefold fewer cells than the wing, and this is the axis that sets that number - so this route separates 'how large' from 'what kind', which is exactly the distinction a wing-number redesign keeps conflating.
routes.mechanism: Ubx limits haltere size by restricting both the transcription and the mobility of Dpp, raising the receptor thickveins and, with engrailed, repressing the glypican dally in the posterior compartment.
routes.reversibility: Depends on the reagent; a conditional allele makes it reversible, a deletion does not.
routes.lethality_risk: Low to moderate. Dpp is used everywhere, so the restriction to the haltere pouch is the whole safety argument.

evidence.cite: Crickmore MA et al. 2006, Science 313:63-8, 'Hox control of organ size by regulation of morphogen production and mobility'
evidence.finding: Ubx 'controls haltere size by restricting both the transcription and the mobility of the morphogen Decapentaplegic (Dpp)' and 'restricts Dpp's distribution in the haltere by increasing the amounts of the Dpp receptor, thickveins'. By the end of larval development the haltere has 'approximately fivefold fewer cells than the wing'.

evidence.cite: Crickmore MA et al. 2007, Development 134:327-34, 'Hox control of morphogen mobility and organ development through regulation of glypican expression'
evidence.finding: Ubx 'modulates morphogen signaling in the haltere through transcriptional regulation of the glypican dally' and, with engrailed, represses dally in the posterior compartment.

evidence.cite: Han C et al. 2005, Development 132:667-79, 'Drosophila glypicans Dally and Dally-like shape the extracellular Wingless morphogen gradient in the wing disc'
evidence.finding: Dally and Dally-like 'are essential and have different roles in Wg gradient formation' in the wing disc - the same glypican machinery, on the other morphogen.

routes.title: Drive the vestigial quadrant enhancer in a segment that has no wing
routes.intervention: Place the vestigial boundary and quadrant enhancers under ectopic control, so that the wing selector is switched on where the two normal signals do not meet.
routes.predicted_phenotype: ECTOPIC WING TISSUE growing out of whatever structure you switched it on in. In Drosophila, vestigial is 'sufficient to induce outgrowths of wing tissue from eyes, legs and antennae' - which is the cleanest demonstration on this page that wing number is not a body-plan constant.
routes.mechanism: vestigial integrates two separate positional signals through two separate enhancers: Notch at the dorsoventral organiser first, then Dpp plus a signal from that organiser in the blade. Bypassing the integration is what makes the outgrowth ectopic.
routes.reversibility: Reversible at the design stage if driven by an inducible system; the outgrowth itself is not.
routes.lethality_risk: Moderate. Wing tissue on an eye or a leg is a welfare and viability problem in its own right.
routes.difficulty: Low. This is a classic, published manipulation.

evidence.cite: Kim J et al. 1996, Nature 382:133-8, 'Integration of positional signals and regulation of wing formation and identity by Drosophila vestigial gene'
evidence.finding: vestigial 'is selectively required for wing-cell proliferation, and is sufficient to induce outgrowths of wing tissue from eyes, legs and antennae'. 'Different signals activate separate enhancers': Notch at the dorsal/ventral organizer, then decapentaplegic plus a signal from that organizer in the blade.

evidence.cite: Williams JA et al. 1994, Nature 368:299-305, 'Organization of wing formation and induction of a wing-patterning gene at the dorsal/ventral compartment boundary'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: The four-winged fly: remove Ubx function from T3
routes.intervention: Combine the classical bithorax-complex alleles - anterobithorax, bithorax, postbithorax - so that T3 is transformed towards T2.
routes.predicted_phenotype: TWO PAIRS OF WINGS, and a fly that is worse at flying than it was - for two reasons that are NOT equally well evidenced, and the page says which is which. The strong one: the transformed T3 has 'only rudimentary indirect flight muscles'. The second pair has no engine. That is direct, quoted, unambiguous insect phenotype. The weaker one: the halteres are gone with it, and the sensory cost of that is real but GRADED, task-dependent and clade-dependent rather than a flat failure - see the sensor scale. So the honest answer is that the swap costs an actuator outright and a sensor partially, to buy a surface.
routes.mechanism: Ubx represses wing identity in T3; removing it lets the T3 disc build a wing. The muscle does not follow, and Fernandes et al. say precisely which step breaks, which is what makes this a design problem rather than a curiosity. Their decomposition: the segmental identity of the EPIDERMIS determines the number of myoblasts on the larval discs and the pattern of their migration during metamorphosis - so those follow the transformation. The segmental identity of the MESODERM is what is crucial for the FUSION of myoblasts into indirect flight muscle, and influences the branching of motor innervation - and the mesoderm is not transformed, because Antp keeps being expressed there. Ectodermal information and autonomous mesodermal homeotic function are BOTH required. So the four-winged fly has the right number of myoblasts, delivered to the right place, that then fail to fuse.
routes.reversibility: Not reversible in the animal. The classical alleles are germline.
routes.lethality_risk: Moderate. The flies are viable; flight is not.
routes.difficulty: Low. These stocks are nearly fifty years old.

evidence.cite: Lewis EB et al. 1978, Nature 276:565-70, 'A gene complex controlling segmentation in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: The bithorax complex 'contains a minimum of eight genes that seem to code for substances controlling levels of thoracic and abdominal development'; repression of at least four is controlled by cis-regulatory elements.

evidence.cite: Fernandes J et al. 1994, Curr Biol 4:957-64, 'Muscle development in the four-winged Drosophila and the role of the Ultrabithorax gene'
evidence.finding: In flies homozygous for anterobithorax, bithorax3 and postbithorax, 'The adults have two pairs of wings, but the homeotically transformed T3 (HT3) has only rudimentary indirect flight muscles'. The decomposition is theirs: 'the segmental identity of the epidermis determines the segment-specific pattern and number of myoblasts on the larval discs, and the pattern of their migration during metamorphosis. The segmental identity of the mesoderm, however, is crucial for the fusion of myoblasts to form indirect flight muscles, and also influences the branching pattern of innervation of indirect flight muscles.' Their conclusion: 'Segmental information expressed in the ectoderm, and the autonomous function of hom[eotic selector genes in the mesoderm]' are both required.

evidence.cite: Roy S et al. 1997, Curr Biol 7:222-7, 'Muscles in the Drosophila second thoracic segment are patterned independently of autonomous homeotic gene function'
evidence.finding: 'Antp continues to be expressed in the mesoderm of the homeotically transformed third thoracic segment in the four-winged fly', which the authors 'suggest ... is a likely reason for the failure of flight muscle development in the transformed segment'.

evidence.cite: Mureli S et al. 2015, J Exp Biol 218:2528-37, 'Haltere mechanosensory influence on tethered flight behavior in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: CITED FOR WHAT IT MEASURED, NOT FOR ITS OPENING PREMISE. The sentence 'Haltere input is necessary for free flight' is this abstract's second sentence and is background - it is there to explain why the experiments are TETHERED ('making it difficult to study the effects of haltere ablation under natural flight conditions'). Their own findings are narrower and partly cut the other way: 'Haltere removal does not affect the flies' ability to flap or steer their wings', and 'intact halteres are not strictly necessary for visually guided wing-steering responses'. What they do show is that haltereless flies 'cannot stabilize a wide-field stimulus as accurately as intact flies can' while they 'fixate figures with the same acuity as intact flies'. See the route sen-haltere-ablation, which carries this in full.

routes.title: Run it backwards: force Ubx in T2 and convert the wing into a haltere
routes.intervention: Express Ubx ectopically in the wing pouch.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A HALTERE-LIKE WING: Wingless signalling and a subset of Wg- and Dpp-activated genes such as spalt-related are repressed, and the blade loses the wing's margin bristles and its veins. A fly with four halteres and no wings does not fly at all, which is the other end of the same axis and is worth putting on the page beside the four-winged one.
routes.mechanism: Ubx acts at several levels of the wing-patterning hierarchy simultaneously, so forcing it in T2 removes the wing programme rather than editing it.
routes.lethality_risk: High for flight; the animal survives, the behaviour does not.

evidence.cite: Weatherbee SD et al. 1998, Genes Dev 12:1474-82, 'Ultrabithorax regulates genes at several levels of the wing-patterning hierarchy to shape the development of the Drosophila haltere'
evidence.finding: 'Ubx represses the expression of the Wingless (Wg) signaling protein and a subset of Wg- and Decapentaplegic-activated genes such as spalt-relat'[ed]. Ubx acts on the wing programme at several levels at once, which is why forcing it in T2 removes that programme rather than editing it. NOTE: the description of a haltere as lacking the wing's margin bristles and veins is Pallavi & Shashidhara's (PMID 16815386), where it is cited; an earlier draft attributed it to this paper, and the quote checker caught it.

evidence.cite: Mohit P et al. 2006, Dev Biol 291:356-67, 'Modulation of AP and DV signaling pathways by the homeotic gene Ultrabithorax during haltere development in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: Microarray analysis of Ubx targets during haltere specification: 'down-regulation of both anterior-posterior and dorso-ventral signaling is critical for haltere fate specification'.

routes.title: Use Antennapedia instead of Ubx, at high dose, to make a wing haltere-like
routes.intervention: Over-express Antp in the wing pouch and raise the dose until the appendage changes.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A HALTERE-LIKE WING at around 490% of endogenous Antp. That threshold is the quantitative test on this page: a Hox dose model calibrated on the Ubx arm alone predicts it, so the two Hox proteins are acting as one repressive 'dose' on one selector rather than as two qualitatively different instructions.
routes.mechanism: Antp and Ubx both repress the Vg-Sd wing selector; Antp is the weaker repressor and is present at roughly a tenth to a twentieth of Ubx's endogenous level, so a large over-expression is needed to reach the same repression.
routes.lethality_risk: Moderate; ectopic Antp is not benign outside the pouch.
routes.difficulty: Moderate: the experiment is only meaningful if the dose is measured, and the two published measurements of the Ubx:Antp ratio in the SAME paper disagree by nearly twofold.

evidence.cite: Paul R et al. 2021, Nat Commun 12:2892, 'Hox dosage contributes to flight appendage morphology in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: Full text read (PMC8129201). 'the wing resembled a haltere in terms of size, shape, and hairs organization when the expression level corresponded to 490% of endogenous Antp'; the paper gives that as five times higher than endogenous Antp. On the Ubx:Antp ratio the paper reports TWO numbers: 'Ubx was 18.5 times more strongly expressed than Antp' by antibody, and 'Ubx expression levels were 10.5 times higher than Antp levels' by matched GFP. It does not leave them in conflict - it attributes the gap to affinity, concluding 'the Antp antibody is 1.85 times less affine' - so the GFP number is the paper's own preferred measurement. Study 1 calibrated both and its GFP arm is the one that predicts the held-out Antp threshold to 4%.

routes.title: Delete vestigial and lose the wing entirely
routes.intervention: Null or wing-specific regulatory mutation of vestigial.
routes.predicted_phenotype: NO WING. vestigial is selectively required for wing-cell proliferation; without it the blade does not grow. This is the negative control for the whole page: it shows the wing is a selector-defined organ, so wing NUMBER is a question about where the selector is switched on.
routes.mechanism: Vestigial partners Scalloped to form the wing selector; Vg binding switches Sd's DNA-target selectivity, so without Vg the same Sd protein reads a different set of sites.
routes.lethality_risk: Low. Wingless flies are viable in the laboratory.

evidence.cite: Kim J et al. 1996, Nature 382:133-8, 'Integration of positional signals and regulation of wing formation and identity by Drosophila vestigial gene'
evidence.finding: vestigial 'is selectively required for wing-cell proliferation'.

evidence.cite: Halder G et al. 1998, Genes Dev 12:3900-9, 'The Vestigial and Scalloped proteins act together to directly regulate wing-specific gene expression in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: Vestigial 'requires the function of the Scalloped protein ... to directly activate the expression of genes involved in wing morphogenesis'.

evidence.cite: Halder G et al. 2001, Development 128:3295-305, 'Binding of the Vestigial co-factor switches the DNA-target selectivity of the Scalloped selector protein'
evidence.finding: 'Binding of Vestigial to Scalloped switches the DNA-binding selectivity of Scalloped' - the selector's specificity is made by the partnership, not by either protein.

evidence.cite: Simmonds AJ et al. 1998, Genes Dev 12:3815-20, 'Molecular interactions between Vestigial and Scalloped promote wing formation in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: Ask what vestigial does in a beetle, where one of the segments is already wingless
routes.intervention: RNAi against vestigial in Tribolium castaneum and in ladybird beetles.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Loss of wing tissue, AND the discovery that the 'wingless' first thoracic segment of a beetle contains two groups of vg-dependent tissues. That matters for a redesign: a segment with no wing is not necessarily a segment with no wing PROGRAMME, so the cheapest place to add a wing may be a segment that already has the latent tissue.
routes.mechanism: vg is a conserved wing gene across insects; ectopic ladybird vg induces wing-like tissue in Drosophila antennae and legs, so the selector is interchangeable across 300 million years.
routes.reversibility: RNAi is transient, so this is among the more reversible routes.
routes.lethality_risk: Low to moderate; the ladybird work found an unexpected requirement in pupal ecdysis, which is a lethality route nobody predicted from the wing phenotype.

evidence.cite: Clark-Hachtel CM et al. 2013, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 110:16951-6, 'Insights into insect wing origin provided by functional analysis of vestigial in the red flour beetle, Tribolium castaneum'
evidence.finding: 'Our investigation in Tribolium (Coleoptera) has revealed that, despite the well-accepted view of vg as an essential wing gene, there are two groups of vg-dependent tissues in the "wingless" first thoracic segment'.

evidence.cite: Ohde T et al. 2009, Insect Mol Biol 18:571-81, 'Vestigial and scalloped in the ladybird beetle: a conserved function in wing development and a novel function in pupal ecdysis'
evidence.finding: 'ectopic expression of H. vigintioctopunctata vg induced wing-like tissues in antennae and legs of D. melanogaster' and larval RNAi 'demonstrated conserved functions of vg and sd in wing development, and an unexpected novel function' in pupal ecdysis.

routes.title: Remove the dorsoventral organiser with apterous and get no wing at all
routes.intervention: Loss of apterous function in the wing disc.
routes.predicted_phenotype: NO WING. apterous specifies dorsal identity and creates the dorsoventral compartment boundary; the organiser at that boundary is what induces the blade. The failure mode is instructive for a designer: you cannot add a wing by adding wing tissue, you add it by creating a BOUNDARY.
routes.mechanism: Dorsal cells expressing apterous meet ventral cells; the interaction at the interface drives wing development.

evidence.cite: Diaz-Benjumea FJ et al. 1993, Cell 75:741-52, 'Interaction between dorsal and ventral cells in the imaginal disc directs wing development in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: 'spatially localized expression of the homeobox gene apterous (ap) specifies the identity of dorsal cells in the wing'; the lineage-restriction boundary 'coincides with the limit of the domain' of ap expression.

evidence.cite: Weihe U et al. 2001, Development 128:4615-22, 'Regulation of Apterous activity in Drosophila wing development'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

evidence.cite: Milán M et al. 2003, Development 130:553-62, 'A re-evaluation of the contributions of Apterous and Notch to the dorsoventral lineage restriction boundary in the Drosophila wing'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

evidence.cite: Delanoue R et al. 2002, Genes Cells 7:1255-66, 'Interaction between apterous and early expression of vestigial in formation of the dorso-ventral compartments in the Drosophila wing disc'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: Attack the hinge rather than the blade, with nubbin
routes.intervention: Wing-disc-specific regulatory mutations of nubbin.
routes.predicted_phenotype: LOSS OF WING STRUCTURES with a localised requirement in the wing HINGE, not the blade. A design that adds wings has to articulate them, and this is the gene that says the hinge is its own growth-control centre rather than the proximal end of the blade's.
routes.mechanism: nubbin encodes a POU-domain transcription factor; mosaic analysis localises its requirement to the hinge, implying a proximal-distal organiser additional to the AP and DV ones.

evidence.cite: Ng M et al. 1995, Development 121:589-99, 'Nubbin encodes a POU-domain protein required for proximal-distal patterning in the Drosophila wing'
evidence.finding: 'Regulatory mutants which selectively remove nubbin expression from wing imaginal discs lead to loss of wing structures'; mosaics suggest 'a localized requirement for nubbin activity in the wing hinge' and 'a novel proximal-distal growth control center in the wing hinge'.

evidence.cite: Rodríguez Dd Ddel A et al. 2002, Development 129:3995-4004, 'Different mechanisms initiate and maintain wingless expression in the Drosophila wing hinge'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: Change hindwing identity in an insect whose hindwing is still a wing
routes.intervention: Perturb Ubx function in butterfly hindwings.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A HINDWING THAT LOOKS MORE LIKE A FOREWING, including its colour pattern. This is the route that separates 'Ubx makes a haltere' from 'Ubx makes a hindwing DIFFERENT': in Lepidoptera the same gene differentiates two flying wings rather than destroying one, which is the existence proof that a four-winged redesign is reachable without losing an aerofoil.
routes.mechanism: Hox genes are transcription factors, so appendage diversity can evolve by changing which targets they regulate rather than by changing the Hox gene itself.
routes.difficulty: High: the genetic toolkit is far thinner than Drosophila's.

evidence.cite: Weatherbee SD et al. 1999, Curr Biol 9:109-15, 'Ultrabithorax function in butterfly wings and the evolution of insect wing patterns'
evidence.finding: 'Given that homologous appendage development is controlled by the same Hox gene in different organisms, and that Hox genes are transcription factors, diversity may evolve from changes in the regulation of Hox target genes.' The authors analysed a butterfly homeotic mutant.

evidence.cite: Tomoyasu Y et al. 2017, Curr Opin Insect Sci 19:8-15, 'Ultrabithorax and the evolution of insect forewing/hindwing differentiation'
evidence.finding: A review of Ubx and insect forewing/hindwing differentiation, revisiting 'the Drosophila paradigm' with 'several new insights emerging from recent studies in non-Drosophila insects'.

routes.title: Specify an extra wing field with localised Wingless
routes.intervention: Drive wingless expression ectopically in the second instar, when the wing/body-wall subdivision is made.
routes.predicted_phenotype: AN ADDITIONAL WING FIELD, if the timing is right. Wing specification is a second-instar event, so this route has a window rather than a dose, which is the kind of knob that makes a design reproducible.
routes.mechanism: Localised Wingless protein specifies the wing compartment of the disc, downstream of the apterous-dependent DV subdivision.
routes.difficulty: Moderate; the timing is the hard part.

evidence.cite: Ng M et al. 1996, Nature 381:316-8, 'Specification of the wing by localized expression of wingless protein'
evidence.finding: 'A third major subdivision of the wing disc into wing and body-wall compartments also occurs in the second instar', specified by localised Wingless.

routes.title: Build the organiser from scratch with Notch, Serrate and Delta
routes.intervention: Create an ectopic Notch-activation stripe, by juxtaposing Serrate- and Delta-expressing cells, in a disc with no wing.
routes.predicted_phenotype: AN ECTOPIC WING MARGIN and the outgrowth that follows it. Serrate signals ventrally-to-dorsally and Delta dorsally-to-ventrally, so a designer has two complementary ligands and can place the boundary rather than inherit it.
routes.mechanism: Notch activation at the DV interface turns on the vestigial boundary enhancer, which starts the blade.
routes.lethality_risk: High. Notch is used in nearly every tissue and ectopic activation is oncogenic in many of them.

routes.title: Reshape the wing by reshaping the Dpp gradient
routes.intervention: Alter Dpp production, receptor level or glypican availability to change the gradient's range.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A LARGER OR SMALLER BLADE with its target genes re-positioned: optomotor-blind and spalt are activated at different distances from the source, so moving the gradient moves the landmarks the venation is built on. This is the knob that changes wing AREA, which study 3 shows is the only aerodynamically profitable thing about adding wings in the first place.
routes.mechanism: Dpp acts directly and at long range; receptor levels themselves shape the gradient, so the tissue is not a passive medium.

routes.title: Replace the wing selector's co-factor with its human ortholog
routes.intervention: Substitute TONDU, the human relative of Vestigial, for Vg function in Drosophila wing formation.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A NORMAL WING, built with a human protein in place of the fly's own. TONDU 'substitutes for Vg function in wing formation'. For a design space this is the load-bearing fact: the wing selector is a module with an interface, and the interface has survived the whole bilaterian radiation, so a redesign can swap parts rather than rebuild them.
routes.mechanism: TONDU interacts with vertebrate TEF factors, the vertebrate relatives of Scalloped, and the Vg-Sd interface is conserved well enough for the substitution to work in vivo.

routes.title: Lift the Ubx brake on EGFR/Ras in the haltere
routes.intervention: Restore EGFR/Ras pathway activity in the haltere disc while leaving Ubx in place.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A HALTERE WITH WING-LIKE CUTICLE AND VEINS, approached from the pathway side rather than the selector side. Wing and haltere epithelia differ in 'the size, shape, spacing and number of cuticular hairs' as well as in veins, so this route separates surface differentiation from appendage identity.
routes.mechanism: Ubx negatively regulates the Egfr/Ras pathway during haltere development; the haltere's lack of veins is partly an EGFR phenotype rather than an identity phenotype.
routes.lethality_risk: Moderate: Ras pathway gain of function is proliferative.

routes.title: Change vein number through rhomboid and the EGFR amplification loop
routes.intervention: Alter rhomboid expression, or EGFR pathway gain, in the larval wing disc.
routes.predicted_phenotype: MORE OR FEWER LONGITUDINAL VEINS, and ectopic vein material where rhomboid is switched on. rhomboid 'mediates the localized formation of wing veins' and is the amplifier that commits a provein cell.
routes.mechanism: rhomboid, with vein, initiates and amplifies DER (EGFR) activity in vein cells through a positive feedback loop in larval stages; late down-regulation of DER then differentiates them.
routes.lethality_risk: Low for the wing; EGFR is pleiotropic elsewhere.

routes.title: Narrow or widen the veins with Delta-Notch lateral inhibition
routes.intervention: Alter Delta or Notch activity in the pupal wing during the 22-30 hour window after puparium formation.
routes.predicted_phenotype: VEINS OF THE WRONG WIDTH, or vein and intervein fates mis-partitioned within the provein. This is the mechanism our venation model is a caricature of: Delta is higher in central provein cells and Notch higher in lateral ones, which is lateral inhibition refining a stripe.
routes.mechanism: Delta-mediated signalling from presumptive vein cells accumulates Notch in presumptive intervein cells; the partitioning depends on that feedback, in a defined time window.
routes.reversibility: Reversible if induced in the window.
routes.difficulty: Low to moderate; the window is narrow.

evidence.cite: Huppert SS et al. 1997, Development 124:3283-91, 'Feedback regulation is central to Delta-Notch signalling required for Drosophila wing vein morphogenesis'
evidence.finding: 'Delta and Notch are required for partitioning of vein and intervein cell fates within the provein during Drosophila metamorphosis', 'dependent on Delta-mediated signalling from 22 to 30 hours after puparium formation at 25 degrees C'. Delta is higher in central provein cells and Notch higher in lateral ones.

evidence.cite: Blair SS et al. 2007, Annu Rev Cell Dev Biol 23:293-319, 'Wing vein patterning in Drosophila and the analysis of intercellular signaling'
evidence.finding: A review of wing vein patterning: positioning and elaboration 'rely on widely utilized developmental signals, including those mediated by EGF, BMP, Hedgehog, Notch, and Wnt' - a combination of short-range and long-range signalling.

routes.title: Move a vein rather than adding one, with Hedgehog
routes.intervention: Shift the Hedgehog-dependent sectors of the anterior compartment and ask where L3 and L4 end up.
routes.predicted_phenotype: VEINS IN DIFFERENT PLACES, same number. This is the route that distinguishes POSITION from COUNT, and it is why our reaction-diffusion model of venation can only speak to the second: a Turing mechanism sets a spacing, and Hedgehog sets an address.
routes.mechanism: Vein primordia form at boundaries between discrete sectors of gene expression along the anteroposterior axis; narrow primordia form first and produce short-range signals that recruit neighbours.

evidence.cite: Crozatier M et al. 2003, Mech Dev 120:529-35, 'Vein-positioning in the Drosophila wing in response to Hh; new roles of Notch signaling'
evidence.finding: 'vein primordia form at boundaries between discrete sectors of gene expression along the antero-posterior (A/P) axis'; rhomboid 'is expressed at the centre of wider vein-competent domains', suggesting 'narrow vein primordia form first, and produce secondary short-range signals'.

routes.title: Attack the intervein instead: blistered / DSRF
routes.intervention: Remove or over-express the Drosophila Serum Response Factor in the pupal wing.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A BLISTERED WING - the two epithelial sheets fail to appose - or ectopic vein where intervein should be. For a design this is the structural failure mode: a wing is two sheets glued together, and the glue is a cell fate.
routes.mechanism: DSRF is expressed in future intervein tissue and is required for its differentiation; it is allelic to blistered.

evidence.cite: Montagne J et al. 1996, Development 122:2589-97, 'The Drosophila Serum Response Factor gene is required for the formation of intervein tissue of the wing and is allelic to blistered'
evidence.finding: 'The Drosophila homolog of the mammalian Serum Response Factor gene (DSRF) ... is expressed in the future intervein tissue of wing imaginal discs' and is 'allelic to blistered'.
