routes.title: Give the four-winged fly an engine: restore indirect flight muscle in the transformed T3
routes.intervention: Transform the T3 MESODERM as well as the ectoderm, by either of two directions nobody has reported: remove Antp function specifically in T3 mesoderm, or drive the T2 mesodermal state there - while keeping the bithorax ectodermal transformation. The target is one named step, myoblast FUSION, not 'muscle' in general.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A SECOND PAIR OF DRIVEN WINGS - the route that would make a four-winged fly actually fly, and NOBODY HAS REPORTED DOING IT. The two ingredients are published separately: the transformed T3 has only rudimentary indirect flight muscles, and Antp persisting in T3 mesoderm is the suggested cause. Specifically ectopic homeotic expression in T2 mesoderm respecifies its muscle pattern, so the mesodermal switch is known to be sufficient in the other direction. Nobody has reported running it in this one.
routes.mechanism: Fernandes et al. split indirect-flight-muscle development into four events and assign each to a germ layer. Myoblast NUMBER on the larval disc and their MIGRATION during metamorphosis follow the EPIDERMIS, which the bithorax alleles do transform. Myoblast FUSION into adult indirect flight muscle, and the branching of motor innervation, follow the MESODERM, which they do not. So exactly one step is broken and it is identified. T2 is the one thoracic segment whose mesoderm expresses no known Antp- or bithorax-complex selector, and its muscle identity is specified entirely by induction; T3 mesoderm expresses Antp autonomously, and that autonomy is what the ectodermal transformation does not reach. The prediction a designer can test is therefore specific: co-transform the mesoderm and the myoblasts that are already in the right place in the right number should fuse.
routes.reversibility: Not reversible in the animal if germline.
routes.lethality_risk: Unknown. Nobody has reported the combination.
routes.difficulty: High, and it is the most interesting route on the page for exactly that reason: the parts are all published and the assembly is not.

evidence.cite: Fernandes J et al. 1994, Curr Biol 4:957-64, 'Muscle development in the four-winged Drosophila and the role of the Ultrabithorax gene'
evidence.finding: 'the homeotically transformed T3 (HT3) has only rudimentary indirect flight muscles'; 'the segmental identity of the mesoderm ... is crucial for the fusion of myoblasts to form indirect flight muscles, and also influences the branching pattern of innervation'.

evidence.cite: Roy S et al. 1997, Curr Biol 7:222-7, 'Muscles in the Drosophila second thoracic segment are patterned independently of autonomous homeotic gene function'
evidence.finding: 'the mesoderm of the second thoracic segment does not express any known homeotic selector gene of the Antp or bithorax complex'; 'specific ectopic expression of Antp and other homeotic selector genes in the mesoderm of the second thoracic segment respecified its muscle pattern'; and Antp persists in transformed-T3 mesoderm, 'a likely reason for the failure of flight muscle development'.

routes.title: Redesign the gearbox: the wing hinge sclerites
routes.intervention: Drive or silence individual control muscles acting on the hinge sclerites and read the resulting wing motion.
routes.predicted_phenotype: SPECIFIC, PREDICTABLE CHANGES IN WING MOTION. The hinge 'transforms tiny, high-frequency oscillations of specialized power muscles into the sweeping back-and-forth motion of the wings', and a trained model now predicts wing motion from steering-muscle activity and attributes it to individual sclerites. If you want a differently-moving wing, this is a far shorter path than a differently-built one.
routes.mechanism: The hinge is a system of hardened sclerites joined flexibly and regulated by specialised control muscles; the four skeletal elements at the wing base are organised with a 'remarkably efficient logic'.
routes.reversibility: Fully reversible: this is stimulation and imaging, not a germline change.
routes.difficulty: High. It needs calcium imaging in flying animals and a dynamically scaled robot to calibrate the forces.

evidence.cite: Melis JM et al. 2024, Nature 628:795-803, 'Machine learning reveals the control mechanics of an insect wing hinge'
evidence.finding: The hinge 'transforms tiny, high-frequency oscillations of specialized power muscles into the sweeping back-and-forth motion of the wings'. A convolutional network 'accurately predicts wing motion from the activity of the steering muscles', an encoder-decoder predicts 'the role of the individual sclerites', and a physics-based simulation 'generates flight manoeuvres that are remarkably similar to those of free-flying flies'.

evidence.cite: Lindsay T et al. 2017, Curr Biol 27:345-358, 'The Function and Organization of the Motor System Controlling Flight Maneuvers in Flies'
evidence.finding: Imaging 'a complete ensemble of wing control muscles in intact, flying flies' uncovered 'a remarkably efficient logic' at the four skeletal elements of the wing base.

routes.title: Use the tension muscles: tp1 and the indirect steering system
routes.intervention: Manipulate indirect steering (tension) muscles, which alter thoracic mechanics rather than pulling on the hinge directly.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A CHANGE IN FLIGHT STABILISATION without touching the direct steering muscles. Connectome data show the indirect steering muscles receive some of the same synaptic input from the sensory apparatus as the direct ones, which makes them a second, parallel actuator for the same control loop.
routes.mechanism: Tension muscles change the mechanical properties of the thorax, so they act on the resonant system rather than on the stroke directly.

evidence.cite: Teoh HK et al. 2025, bioRxiv, 'How tp1, an indirect wing steering muscle, stabilizes Drosophila's flight'
evidence.finding: 'Flapping flight is inherently unstable, requiring Drosophila to fine-tune their wing motions on a milliseconds timescale.' Connectome data 'reveal that indirect steering muscles or tension muscles, which alter the mechanics of the thorax, receive some of the same synaptic inputs from the sensory apparatus as the direct steering muscles'. PREPRINT: this is a bioRxiv record, not a peer-reviewed paper, and the page says so.

routes.title: Re-tune the thorax: the scutellum and sub-epimeral ridge
routes.intervention: Lesion the exoskeletal linkages that couple left wing to right wing (scutellum) and wing to haltere (sub-epimeral ridge).
routes.predicted_phenotype: DESYNCHRONISED WINGS AND HALTERES, and a thorax whose resonant frequency no longer responds normally to wing damage. This is the route that shows wingbeat frequency is not a free parameter a designer can set: it is a property of wing-thorax resonance, and clipping wings raises it 'by as much as 90 Hz'.
routes.mechanism: Wings and halteres are independently driven, coupled oscillators. The wing-wing system is strongly coupled; the wing-haltere system is weakly and UNIDIRECTIONALLY coupled - changing wingbeat frequency moves haltere frequency, but loading the haltere does not move the wings.
routes.reversibility: Not reversible: this is surgery on the exoskeleton.
routes.lethality_risk: Low for survival, high for flight.

evidence.cite: Deora T et al. 2021, Elife 10, 'Wings and halteres act as coupled dual oscillators in flies'
evidence.finding: Full text read. 'Wings and halteres are independently driven, coupled oscillators'; the wing-haltere link 'acts in a unidirectional manner; altering wingbeat frequency affects haltere frequency, but not vice versa'. 'In insects with an intact thorax, clipping the wings increases wingbeat frequency by as much as 90 Hz.' The haltere 'is powered by a single asynchronous muscle whose contractions activate its upstroke, whereas the downstroke is thought to be entirely passive'.

routes.title: Remove the halteres and measure what flight loses
routes.intervention: Bilateral or unilateral haltere ablation, or reduction of haltere mass, in tethered and free flight.
routes.predicted_phenotype: LOSS OF EQUILIBRIUM REFLEXES - but a GRADED and TASK-SPECIFIC loss, not a flat failure, and the page is careful about this because it is easy to overstate. What is measured: angular rotations normally elicit compensatory changes in stroke amplitude and frequency, and uni- and bilateral ablation removes them (Dickinson 1999). Haltereless flies cannot stabilise a WIDE-FIELD stimulus as accurately, yet fixate FIGURES with the same acuity, and can still flap and steer (Mureli & Fox 2015). Takeoff velocity and stability fall in Calyptratae and NOT in other flies (Yarger 2021). The flat claim 'haltere input is necessary for free flight' appears in this literature as a PREMISE sentence rather than as a measured result, and we did not find the free-flight ablation measurement it stands on - see `not_claimed` at the top level of this file.
routes.mechanism: Halteres encode angular velocity by detecting the Coriolis forces produced by their own linear oscillation inside the rotating frame of the thorax. The directional tuning is close to linear, so the responses vary as simple trigonometric functions of stimulus orientation.
routes.reversibility: Not reversible: the organ does not grow back.
routes.lethality_risk: Low for survival; severe for flight.
routes.difficulty: Low. This is the oldest experiment in the field.

evidence.cite: Dickinson MH et al. 1999, Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci 354:903-16, 'Haltere-mediated equilibrium reflexes of the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster'
evidence.finding: 'flies possess a robust equilibrium reflex in which angular rotations of the body elicit compensatory changes in both the amplitude and stroke frequency of the wings'; ablation experiments 'demonstrate that the halteres are required for these stability reflexes'. The reflexes 'function primarily to stabilize pitch and yaw within the horizontal plane'.

evidence.cite: Mureli S et al. 2015, J Exp Biol 218:2528-37, 'Haltere mechanosensory influence on tethered flight behavior in Drosophila'
evidence.finding: Their PREMISE, flagged as such: 'Haltere input is necessary for free flight, making it difficult to study the effects of haltere ablation under natural flight conditions' - which is why the work is tethered. Their RESULTS: 'Haltere removal does not affect the flies' ability to flap or steer their wings, but it does increase the temporal frequency at which they modify their wingbeat amplitude'; 'Reducing the haltere mass decreases the optomotor reflex response to wide-field motion, and removing the haltere entirely does not further decrease the response'; 'Decreasing the mass does not attenuate the response to figure motion, but removing the entire haltere does attenuate the response'; haltereless flies 'fixate figures with the same acuity as intact flies, but cannot stabilize a wide-field stimulus as accurately as intact flies can'. Their own conclusion is a qualifier: 'during tethered flight, intact halteres are not strictly necessary for visually guided wing-steering responses'.

evidence.cite: Nalbach G et al. 1994, Neuroscience 61:149-63, 'Extremely non-orthogonal axes in a sense organ for rotation: behavioural analysis of the dipteran haltere system'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: Delete the sensor by DEGREES: graded silencing of haltere campaniform sensilla
routes.intervention: Use Gal4 driver lines expressed in different populations of haltere campaniform neurons to silence or ablate an increasing number of them.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A LINEAR DECLINE in the magnitude of wing and head motor responses to yaw rotation as more sensilla are silenced. This is the route that turns 'the haltere is necessary' into a dose-response, and it is the sensory analogue of the Hox dose experiment in study 1: the same question - switch or dial - asked of the sensor rather than the selector.
routes.mechanism: Each haltere carries hundreds of strain-sensing campaniform sensilla that encode forces at the organ's base as it oscillates; the equilibrium reflex is the population's output.
routes.reversibility: Genetic silencing is reversible in principle; ablation is not.
routes.difficulty: Moderate; the driver lines are the hard part and they exist.

evidence.cite: Sharma T et al. 2026, J Exp Biol 229, 'The role of haltere campaniform sensilla in equilibrium reflexes of the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster'
evidence.finding: 'the magnitude of the wing and head motor responses of flies decreases linearly with an increasing number of campaniform sensilla genetically silenced or ablated, providing direct evidence for the involvement of these mechanosensory structures in the detection of angular velocity during flight'. The paper opens by noting that the requirement of the campaniform sensilla themselves 'has yet to be directly demonstrated'.

evidence.cite: Yarger AM et al. 2018, Proc Biol Sci 285, 'Single mechanosensory neurons encode lateral displacements using precise spike timing and thresholds'
evidence.finding: Single haltere mechanosensory neurons 'encode lateral displacements using precise spike timing and thresholds'.

evidence.cite: Fox JL et al. 2008, J Comp Physiol A Neuroethol Sens Neural Behav Physiol 194:887-97, 'A neural basis for gyroscopic force measurement in the halteres of Holorusia'
evidence.finding: A neural basis for gyroscopic force measurement in the halteres of the crane fly Holorusia: Coriolis forces 'occur at oscillation frequency and twice the oscillation frequency', and this is single-fibre recording from primary afferents.

routes.title: Treat the haltere as an output, not just an input
routes.intervention: Modulate the haltere's own control muscles and measure the effect on wing steering muscle timing.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A CHANGE IN WING MOTOR NEURON SPIKE TIMING - i.e. steering - produced by moving the SENSOR rather than the wing. This is the finding that most undermines the simple story the page starts from: the haltere is not only a gyroscope being read, it is 'an adjustable clock' being set, and visual input reaches it.
routes.mechanism: Haltere motor neurons receive strong excitatory input from directionally sensitive visual interneurons; descending visual input modulates haltere muscle activity, which alters the mechanosensory feedback that regulates the wing steering muscles.

evidence.cite: Dickerson BH et al. 2019, Curr Biol 29:3517-3524.e3, 'Flies Regulate Wing Motion via Active Control of a Dual-Function Gyroscope'
evidence.finding: 'rather than acting solely as a gyroscope to detect body rotation, halteres also function as an adjustable clock to set the spike timing of wing motor neurons, a specialized capability that evolved from the generic flight circuitry of their four-winged ancestors'.

evidence.cite: Chan WP et al. 1998, Science 280:289-92, 'Visual input to the efferent control system of a fly's "gyroscope"'
evidence.finding: 'motoneurons innervating muscles of the haltere receive strong excitatory input from directionally sensitive visual interneurons'.

evidence.cite: Fayyazuddin A et al. 1996, J Neurosci 16:5225-32, 'Haltere afferents provide direct, electrotonic input to a steering motor neuron in the blowfly, Calliphora'
evidence.finding: The b1 steering motor neuron 'fires a single phase-locked spike during each wingbeat cycle', thought to result from wingbeat-synchronous mechanosensory input; haltere afferents provide DIRECT, ELECTROTONIC input to it - i.e. the fastest connection anatomy allows.

routes.title: Substitute the missing gyro: use the WING's own campaniform sensilla
routes.intervention: In an insect with no halteres, perturb the campaniform sensilla on the wings themselves and measure flight posture control.
routes.predicted_phenotype: LOSS OF POSTURAL CONTROL in a moth, from a wing sensor rather than a haltere. This is the route that says a four-winged redesign need not be flying blind: the same class of mechanoreceptor sits on the wing, and in Lepidoptera it already does the job. Whether a fly could be made to use its wing sensilla the way a moth does is, as far as we found, untested.
routes.mechanism: Campaniform sensilla are the same strain-sensing structures found on halteres; they are also present on wings, where they can encode the forces a wing experiences.

evidence.cite: Dickerson BH et al. 2014, J Exp Biol 217:2301-8, 'Control of moth flight posture is mediated by wing mechanosensory feedback'
evidence.finding: 'Insect halteres are mechanosensory organs that encode inertial forces ... but serve no aerodynamic role and are specific to two orders of insects (Diptera and Strepsiptera).' 'The mechanosensory structures found on the halteres, campaniform sensilla, are also present' on wings, and moth flight posture is mediated by wing mechanosensory feedback.

routes.title: Detune the sensor without removing it: load the haltere knob
routes.intervention: Add small calibrated masses to the haltere end-knob and measure haltere and wingbeat frequency.
routes.predicted_phenotype: HALTERE FREQUENCY FALLS IN DISCRETE STEPS above a threshold load while WINGBEAT FREQUENCY DOES NOT MOVE - and the effect reverses when the load is removed. A reversible, graded, non-genetic way to break the rate gyro, which makes it the best control experiment on this page for 'is it the sensing, or is it the mass?'.
routes.mechanism: The sub-epimeral ridge couples the two oscillators unidirectionally, so a change on the haltere side does not propagate back to the wings.
routes.reversibility: FULLY reversible, and demonstrated to be: detaching the load restored haltere frequency.

evidence.cite: Deora T et al. 2021, Elife 10, 'Wings and halteres act as coupled dual oscillators in flies'
evidence.finding: Full text read. 'Small loads did not affect haltere frequency, but as the load increased beyond a threshold, haltere frequency decreased in discrete steps. However, wingbeat frequency remained constant in these experiments.' 'we detached the load and confirmed that haltere frequency recovered and again matched wingbeat frequency'.

routes.title: Count what converting a haltere into a wing actually spends
routes.intervention: None - this is an accounting route. Take any route that transforms T3 towards T2 and ask what sensory capability leaves with the haltere.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A FLY WITH NO RATE GYRO. Every route on this page that produces a second pair of wings also produces this, and the literature nowhere reports a four-winged fly that kept its halteres. Our own model (study 3) puts the boundary at a feedback loop of about 3 wingbeats, roughly 14 ms: slower than that and the measured 60 ms recovery is unreachable AT ANY GAIN. The haltere loop is inside that boundary and the visual loop, at about 30 ms, is well outside it.
routes.mechanism: The haltere IS the hindwing. There is no version of 'convert the hindwing into a wing' that keeps it.
routes.difficulty: Not applicable; this is the arithmetic, and it is the point of the page.

evidence.cite: Sherman A et al. 2003, J Exp Biol 206:295-302, 'A comparison of visual and haltere-mediated equilibrium reflexes in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster'
evidence.finding: 'the visual system is tuned to relatively slow rotation whereas the haltere-mediated respo[nse]' is tuned faster - the two modalities differ in their mechanisms of transduction and therefore in their temporal responses.

evidence.cite: Ristroph L et al. 2010, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 107:4820-4, 'Discovering the flight autostabilizer of fruit flies by inducing aerial stumbles'
evidence.finding: Flies 'respond to gentle disturbances by accurately returning to their original orientation', taking 'advantage of a stabilizing aerodynamic influence and active torque generation to recover their heading to within 2 degrees in < 60 ms'.

evidence.cite: Sherman A et al. 2004, J Exp Biol 207:133-42, 'Summation of visual and mechanosensory feedback in Drosophila flight control'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: Skip the genetics: steer the insect with an implanted radio stimulator
routes.intervention: Implant a radio-equipped neural and muscular stimulator and drive flight initiation, cessation, elevation and turning.
routes.predicted_phenotype: CONTROLLED FLIGHT IN A FREE-FLYING BEETLE. Flight initiation, cessation and elevation through brain stimulation; turns through direct stimulation of either basalar muscle. If the goal is a redesigned flight apparatus that does something new, this is the only route on the page that has already produced a steerable animal, and it required no change to any gene.
routes.mechanism: The flight motor is addressable: the brain carries the start/stop decision and individual steering muscles carry the turn, so an electrode at each gives open-loop control.
routes.reversibility: The implant is removable; the implantation is not.
routes.lethality_risk: Moderate. This is surgery on a living animal and the welfare section below treats it as the page's most ethically loaded route.
routes.difficulty: Moderate, and falling: the hardware is now commodity.

evidence.cite: Sato H et al. 2009, Front Integr Neurosci 3:24, 'Remote radio control of insect flight'
evidence.finding: 'We demonstrated the remote control of insects in free flight via an implantable radio-equipped miniature neural stimulating system.' 'Flight initiation, cessation and elevation control were accomplished through neural stimulus of the brain ... Turns were triggered through the direct muscular stimulus of either of the basalar muscles.'

evidence.cite: Sato H et al. 2015, Curr Biol 25:798-803, 'Deciphering the role of a coleopteran steering muscle via free flight stimulation'
evidence.finding: Free-flight stimulation used to decipher the role of a coleopteran steering muscle: 'The inability to stimulate in free flight has been a long-standing hurdle for insect flight studies.'

evidence.cite: Vo-Doan TT et al. 2022, Cyborg Bionic Syst 2022:9780504, 'A Cyborg Insect Reveals a Function of a Muscle in Free Flight'
evidence.finding: An insect-computer hybrid robot: a wireless backpack controller on a living beetle, used to reveal a muscle's function in free flight.

evidence.cite: Choo HY et al. 2016, PLoS One 11:e0151808, 'Electrical Stimulation of Coleopteran Muscle for Initiating Flight'
evidence.finding: Electrical stimulation of coleopteran muscle to obtain 'a reliable and controllable flight initiation protocol'.

evidence.cite: Sato H et al. 2010, Front Neurosci 4:199, 'Recent developments in the remote radio control of insect flight'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: The same trick on a small insect: optic-lobe stimulation in a honeybee
routes.intervention: Apply electrical stimulation to the optic lobes of a honeybee and attempt steering, not just start/stop.
routes.predicted_phenotype: STEERING, verified experimentally. Optic-lobe stimulation was already established for initiation and cessation in small insects; the open question this addresses is whether the same electrode can turn the animal.
routes.mechanism: Visual interneurons feed the steering circuitry, so stimulating them injects a turn command upstream of the motor.
routes.reversibility: Reversible in the sense that stimulation stops; the implant is not.

evidence.cite: Yu L et al. 2022, Cyborg Bionic Syst 2022:9895837, 'Experimental Verification on Steering Flight of Honeybee by Electrical Stimulation'
evidence.finding: 'The existing research has recognized that the electrical stimulation applied to the optic lobes was an appropriate flight control strategy for small insects represented by honeybee ... However, its regulation effect on steering locomotion has not been fully verified.'

routes.title: Rewire the fusion rule between the fast and the slow sense
routes.intervention: Deliver haltere and visual stimuli separately and together and measure how the wing motor output combines them.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A LINEAR SUM, for wing motor output - but NOT for gaze. That asymmetry is a design constraint: if you intend to compensate for a deleted haltere by upweighting vision, the literature says the two pathways are already summing linearly at the wing, so there is no untapped nonlinearity to exploit; and the head and the wings are not the same control problem.
routes.mechanism: The two modalities converge on the steering motor neurons with different temporal tuning, the visual system tuned to slow rotation and the haltere pathway to fast.

evidence.cite: Rauscher MJ et al. 2021, Proc Biol Sci 288:20202374, 'Haltere and visual inputs sum linearly to predict wing (but not gaze) motor output in tethered flying Drosophila'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

evidence.cite: Sherman A et al. 2003, J Exp Biol 206:295-302, 'A comparison of visual and haltere-mediated equilibrium reflexes in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster'
evidence.finding: 'the visual system is tuned to relatively slow rotation whereas the haltere-mediated respo[nse]' is faster.

evidence.cite: Sherman A et al. 2004, J Exp Biol 207:133-42, 'Summation of visual and mechanosensory feedback in Drosophila flight control'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: Switch wings on and off without changing the genome: the pea aphid polyphenism
routes.intervention: Apply the environmental cue - crowding - and let one genotype build winged or wingless daughters.
routes.predicted_phenotype: WINGED OR WINGLESS OFFSPRING FROM ONE GENOME. This is the only scale on the page where wing number is already a controllable variable in a living animal with no genetic lesion at all, and it is therefore the only route with no lethality and full reversibility.
routes.mechanism: An environmental stressor is transduced into a developmental decision; the genome-wide transcriptional response has been characterised. The proportion of winged females produced varies between clonal genotypes, and in males wing production is instead environmentally insensitive and sex-linked.
routes.reversibility: Completely reversible: it is a generational switch, not a lesion.
routes.difficulty: Low to rear, high to dissect mechanistically.

evidence.cite: Braendle C et al. 2005, Proc Biol Sci 272:657-64, 'Genetic variation for an aphid wing polyphenism is genetically linked to a naturally occurring wing polymorphism'
evidence.finding: 'Winged and wingless phenotypes also occur in males of the sexual generation. In contrast to parthenogenetic females, wing production in males is environmentally insensitive and controlled by the sex-li[nked locus]'; the proportion of winged females 'varies between clonal genotypes'.

evidence.cite: Vellichirammal NN et al. 2016, Mol Ecol 25:4146-60, 'The genomewide transcriptional response underlying the pea aphid wing polyphenism'
evidence.finding: The genome-wide transcriptional response underlying the pea aphid wing polyphenism.

evidence.cite: Grantham ME et al. 2016, Biol Lett 12, 'A case for a joint strategy of diversified bet hedging and plasticity in the pea aphid wing polyphenism'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: Interrupt the wing network at a different point in each species: the ant castes
routes.intervention: Compare expression of the wing-patterning network across winged and wingless castes in several ant species.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A WINGLESS CASTE, with the interruption at a DIFFERENT NODE in each species. For a design space this is the single most useful comparative fact on the page: the network is conserved in the winged castes, and the points at which it is broken in the wingless ones are 'evolutionarily labile' - so there is no one place a wing programme has to be cut, and a designer has many equivalent entry points.
routes.mechanism: Wing polyphenism in ants evolved once, 125 million years ago; the network's conservation and the lability of its interruption points have been simultaneous ever since.
routes.reversibility: Not applicable: this is a developmental programme, not an intervention.

evidence.cite: Abouheif E et al. 2002, Science 297:249-52, 'Evolution of the gene network underlying wing polyphenism in ants'
evidence.finding: 'the expression of several genes within the network is conserved in the winged castes of four ant species, whereas points of interruption within the network in the wingless castes are evolutionarily labile'. Wing polyphenism in ants 'evolved once, 125 million years ago'.

routes.title: Use a hormone receptor as the wing switch: the planthopper insulin pathway
routes.intervention: Manipulate either of the two insulin receptors in Nilaparvata lugens.
routes.predicted_phenotype: LONG-WINGED OR SHORT-WINGED ADULTS, switched by a receptor rather than by a selector gene. Long-winged morphs fly and short-winged ones do not but are usually more fecund, which is the clearest statement anywhere on this page of what flight costs.
routes.mechanism: Two insulin receptors determine the alternative morphs, downstream of nutritional status.
routes.reversibility: RNAi is transient; the morph, once built, is not.

evidence.cite: Xu HJ et al. 2015, Nature 519:464-7, 'Two insulin receptors determine alternative wing morphs in planthoppers'
evidence.finding: 'Long-winged morphs can fly, which allows them to escape adverse habitats and track changing resources, whereas short-winged morphs are flightless, but usually possess higher fecundity than the winged morphs.' Two insulin receptors determine the alternative morphs.

evidence.cite: Xu HJ et al. 2017, Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci 372, 'Insulin receptors and wing dimorphism in rice planthoppers'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

evidence.cite: Li X et al. 2021, Insect Sci 28:1300-1313, 'An InR/mir-9a/NlUbx regulatory cascade regulates wing diphenism in brown planthoppers'
evidence.finding: NOT READ. The PubMed record for this paper resolves and its title and journal are as cited; we have read none of its results and make no claim from it beyond what its title states.

routes.title: The same Hox gene, used as a morph switch instead of an identity switch
routes.intervention: RNAi against Ultrabithorax in short-winged planthopper nymphs.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A WING-LENGTH CHANGE rather than a wing-identity change. In planthoppers Ubx is expressed in BOTH forewing and hindwing pads - 'different from the canonical model of Ubx expression' - and is regulated by the nutritional status of the host plant. The same protein that deletes a wing pair in a fly tunes wing LENGTH in a bug, which is the strongest warning on this page against reading a Drosophila Hox phenotype as a general rule.
routes.mechanism: NlUbx responds to host-plant quality and switches between the migratory long-winged and the reproductive short-winged form.

evidence.cite: Liu F et al. 2020, Natl Sci Rev 7:1181-1189, 'Ultrabithorax is a key regulator for the dimorphism of wings, a main cause for the outbreak of planthoppers in rice'
evidence.finding: 'Ubx is expressed in both forewing and hindwing pads, which is different from the canonical model of Ubx expression. In brown planthoppers, expression of Ubx (NlUbx) is regulated by nutritional status of the rice host.'

evidence.cite: Fu SJ et al. 2020, Gene 737:144446, 'Functional analysis of Ultrabithorax in the wing-dimorphic planthopper Nilaparvata lugens (Stål, 1854) (Hemiptera: Delphacidae)'
evidence.finding: 'RNA-interference (RNAi)-mediated silencing of NlUbx in short-winged BPH nymphs significantly induc[ed]' a change; two NlUbx isoforms were identified.

routes.title: Turn the haltere feedback up and down, and ask whether vision can do the same job
routes.intervention: On a magnetic tether, where the fly is fixed in space but FREE TO ROTATE about its yaw axis, manipulate haltere-mediated feedback and visual feedback separately and measure the dynamics of body saccades.
routes.predicted_phenotype: SACCADE AMPLITUDE TRACKS THE HALTERE AND IGNORES VISION. Increasing haltere-mediated feedback decreases saccade amplitude and decreasing it increases amplitude, while altering visual feedback has no significant effect on saccade dynamics at all. This is the cleanest measured statement on the page that the two senses are not interchangeable, and it is GRADED rather than all-or-nothing - which is what an ablation experiment cannot show.
routes.mechanism: The two modalities are sensitive to different angular velocity bands. The haltere system dominates the fast rotations a saccade consists of; the visual system contributes at lower angular velocities, to which the haltere system is less sensitive.
routes.reversibility: Fully reversible: the manipulations are feedback settings on a tether, not lesions.
routes.difficulty: Moderate. A magnetic tether is a standard rig.

evidence.cite: Bender JA et al. 2006, J Exp Biol 209:4597-606, 'A comparison of visual and haltere-mediated feedback in the control of body saccades in Drosophila melanogaster'
evidence.finding: 'altering visual feedback had no significant effect on the dynamics of saccades, whereas increasing and decreasing the amount of haltere-mediated feedback decreased and increased saccade amplitude, respectively'. And the complement: 'the visual system does provide feedback for flight stability at lower angular velocities, to which the haltere system is less sensitive'. Note the rig: a magnetic tether leaves 'flies ... fixed in space but free to rotate about their yaw axis', which is closer to free flight than a rigid tether and still not free flight.

evidence.cite: Sherman A et al. 2003, J Exp Biol 206:295-302, 'A comparison of visual and haltere-mediated equilibrium reflexes in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster'
evidence.finding: 'the visual system is tuned to relatively slow rotation whereas the haltere-mediated respo[nse]' is faster - the mechanism behind the result above.

routes.title: Measure the delay-versus-gain trade-off directly, on a robot
routes.intervention: Run a dynamically scaled robotic fruit fly with a real-time proportional controller on yaw velocity, and sweep the feedback delay across the range a real fly experiences.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A HARD TRADE-OFF BETWEEN SENSOR DELAY AND PERMISSIBLE GAIN: the longer the delay, the lower the gain the system tolerates, so a slow sense cannot be compensated by turning it up. This route exists on the page because it is PRIOR ART for our own study 3, which rediscovered the same trade-off in simulation and put the usable-delay boundary at about 3 wingbeats. Our result is a re-derivation, not a discovery, and the page says so.
routes.mechanism: Fast mechanosensory feedback provides active damping that complements the passive damping of flapping itself; a haltere-mediated inner loop supplies that damping for a slower, visually mediated outer loop.
routes.difficulty: High. It needs a dynamically scaled robotic fly with real-time torque feedback.

evidence.cite: Elzinga MJ et al. 2012, J R Soc Interface 9:1685-96, 'The influence of sensory delay on the yaw dynamics of a flapping insect'
evidence.finding: 'The results show a fundamental trade-off between sensor delay and permissible feedback gain, and suggest that fast mechanosensory feedback in flies, and most probably in other insects, provide a source of active damping which compliments that contributed by passive effects.' Their proposed architecture is the one study 3 assumes: 'a haltere-mediated inner-loop proportional controller provides damping for slower visually mediated feedback'. NOTE: this is a robot and a model, not an animal - the evidence class is model_only even though the apparatus is physical.

evidence.cite: Chang S et al. 2014, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 111:11246-51, 'Predicting fruit fly's sensing rate with insect flight simulations'
evidence.finding: A free-flight simulation giving 'theoretical bounds on both the sensing rate and the delay time between sensing and actuation', from which the authors 'conjecture that fruit flies sense their kinematic states every wing beat to stabilize their flight', and propose 'the fly's haltere and first basalar motor neuron' as the candidate pathway. A conjecture, in their word, not a measurement.

routes.title: Count what else the haltere is doing before you spend it
routes.intervention: Ablate halteres and measure NON-flight behaviours: walking speed on vertical surfaces, response to sudden changes in gravity, and postural stabilisation while standing.
routes.predicted_phenotype: DEGRADED WALKING AND STANDING, in an animal that is not flying. Intact halteres are necessary to maintain normal walking speeds on vertical surfaces and to respond to sudden changes in gravity; crane flies with ablated halteres show reduced postural stability against perturbations and need longer to recover. This is a cost no flight model on this page counts, including ours, and it is charged to every route that converts a haltere into a wing.
routes.mechanism: The haltere is an inertial sensor, and inertial information is useful whenever the body is being accelerated - which is not only in flight. Several taxa oscillate their halteres while walking.

evidence.cite: Daltorio KA et al. 2018, J Exp Biol 221, 'Haltere removal alters responses to gravity in standing flies'
evidence.finding: 'We found that intact halteres are necessary for flies to maintain normal walking speeds on vertical surfaces and to respond to sudden changes in gravity. Our results suggest that halteres can serve multiple sensory purposes during different behaviors, expanding their role beyond their canonical use in flight.'

evidence.cite: Lea KM et al. 2026, Curr Biol 36:3103-3113.e3, 'Halteres stabilize standing posture in crane flies'
evidence.finding: In crane flies, 'freely behaving flies with ablated halteres exhibited reduced postural stability against perturbations and required longer recovery times', and haltere oscillations during standing are 'driven by passive displacement of the legs'. The paper's own opening premise - 'Halteres are necessary for flight control in all winged flies' - is background in this paper too, not its result, and is not used here as evidence of that claim.

evidence.cite: Hall JM et al. 2015, Biol Lett 11, 'Kinematic diversity suggests expanded roles for fly halteres'
evidence.finding: Haltere movements during free walking 'were correlated with phylogeny', and the authors 'predicted that haltere removal might decrease behavioural performance in those flies that move them during walking and provide evidence that this is the case'.

routes.title: Copy the animal that already has four independently controlled wings
routes.intervention: None genetic. Study the fore-hind wing phasing of dragonflies and damselflies and ask what a fly would need to replicate it.
routes.predicted_phenotype: FOUR WINGS THAT CAN BE BETTER THAN TWO, at the right phase. Dragonflies 'have maintained their distinctive, independently controllable, four-winged form for over 300 Myr', and fore-hind phasing 'can improve aerodynamic efficiency by removing swirl'. This is the route that keeps the page honest: the answer to 'would four wings fly better' is not simply no.
routes.mechanism: Phasing lets the hindwing recover energy from the forewing's wake instead of flying through disturbed air. The sign of the interaction depends on the phase, which is a CONTROL variable and not a morphological one.
routes.difficulty: The morphology is the easy part. Phasing four wings needs four independent actuators and the control to use them, which is exactly what the homeotic route does NOT deliver.

evidence.cite: Usherwood JR et al. 2008, J R Soc Interface 5:1303-7, 'Phasing of dragonfly wings can improve aerodynamic efficiency by removing swirl'
evidence.finding: 'dragonflies and damselflies have maintained their distinctive, independently controllable, four-winged form for over 300Myr'; previous studies 'have generally painted a rather disappointing picture' of interactions, but phasing 'can improve aerodynamic efficiency by removing swirl'.

evidence.cite: Lai YH et al. 2020, Bioinspir Biomim 16, 'Effect of wing-wing interaction coupled with morphology and kinematic features of damselflies'
evidence.finding: Wing-wing interaction in two damselfly species in forward flight, analysed with high-speed video and 3D numerical simulation: the effects are 'complicated combinations of biological morphology, wing kinematics and fluid dynamics'.

routes.title: Remove the hindwings of an insect that has four, and measure flight
routes.intervention: Cut the hindwings off moths and butterflies and track three-dimensional flight trajectories.
routes.predicted_phenotype: THEY STILL FLY, having lost nearly half their wing area, BUT they lose linear and turning acceleration and can no longer execute normal evasive flight. Turning RADIUS is unaffected; speed is not. This is the single most direct measurement on the page of what a second wing pair actually buys, and the answer is agility, not lift.
routes.mechanism: Lepidopteran flight is anteromotoric: forewings and hindwings are mechanically coupled and flap in synchrony, with the forewings driving. The hindwing is therefore a manoeuvring surface rather than a primary lift surface.
routes.lethality_risk: Low in the laboratory; the paper argues it is lethal in the wild, through bats and birds.

evidence.cite: Jantzen B et al. 2008, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 105:16636-40, 'Hindwings are unnecessary for flight but essential for execution of normal evasive flight in Lepidoptera'
evidence.finding: 'lepidopterans can still fly when their hindwings are cut off, a procedure reducing their total wing surface, on average, by nearly one half.' But 'hindwing removal causes lepidopterans to incur a loss in both linear and turning acceleration'; they 'still are able to zigzag aerially (the ablation has no effect on their turning radius in flight) but at lesser speed and therefore less evasively'.

routes.title: The halteres on the wrong segment: Strepsiptera
routes.intervention: None. Read the one insect order whose haltere-like organs sit on the MESOthorax, the reverse of the dipteran arrangement.
routes.predicted_phenotype: A FLYING INSECT WITH THE HALTERE/WING ARRANGEMENT INVERTED. If the inversion is a homeotic change, then the design the page is discussing - move which segment carries the aerofoil and which carries the gyroscope - has already happened once in evolution, and the animal flies. If the two organs instead arose convergently, it has not. The literature treats this as OPEN, and the page keeps it open.
routes.mechanism: Proposed as 'a radical homeotic mutation' switching the position of wings and halteres, if Strepsiptera are the sister group of Diptera. The alternative affiliation to Coleoptera 'implies that dipteran halteres and strepsipteran haltere-like organs evolved convergently'.

evidence.cite: Rokas A et al. 1999, Insect Mol Biol 8:527-30, 'Intron insertion as a phylogenetic character: the engrailed homeobox of Strepsiptera does not indicate affinity with Diptera'
evidence.finding: 'Affiliation to Coleoptera has been proposed, however this implies that dipteran halteres and strep-sipteran haltere-like organs evolved convergently. An alternative is a sister group relationship with Diptera. In this case, halteres could be homologous but a radical homeotic mutation may have switched their position to the Strepsipteran mesothorax.' This paper's own intron-insertion evidence 'does not indicate affinity with Diptera'.

evidence.cite: Minelli A et al. 2009, BMC Biol 7:36, 'Phylo-evo-devo: combining phylogenetics with evolutionary developmental biology'
evidence.finding: A phylo-evo-devo discussion revisiting 'the inverted positions of wings and halteres in the Diptera and the Strepsiptera in terms of a putative homeotic mutation in the Hox gene Ultrabithorax'.

routes.title: Ask whether halteres are necessary in every fly, and find that they are not
routes.intervention: Remove halteres across dipteran families and measure takeoff velocity and stability.
routes.predicted_phenotype: HALTERE REMOVAL HURTS CALYPTRATAE AND NOT OTHER FLIES. In Calyptratae - house flies and relatives - removal cut both takeoff velocity and stability, through a slower leg extension; in non-Calyptratae, including a closely related species with an equally rapid takeoff, it did neither. What this is NOT in tension with is a competing FINDING. The flat sentence often quoted against it - that haltere input is required for unrestrained flight - recurs in this literature as an opening PREMISE, a reason for tethering the animal or for studying walking, and we found no free-flight ablation measurement behind it. So the picture is not two results in conflict; it is a strong background assumption sitting on top of measured results that are narrower than it, graded by task, and graded by clade. See `not_claimed` at the top level of this file.
routes.mechanism: Calyptratae move their halteres independently of their wings and oscillate them during walking; other flies do not. Haltere kinematic diversity tracks phylogeny.

evidence.cite: Yarger AM et al. 2021, Proc Biol Sci 288:20202375, 'Takeoff diversity in Diptera'
evidence.finding: 'Haltere removal decreased both velocity and stability in the takeoffs of Calyptratae, but not other flies.' 'A closely related non-Calyptratae species ... also has a rapid takeoff, but takeoff duration and stability are unaffected by haltere removal.'

evidence.cite: Hall JM et al. 2015, Biol Lett 11, 'Kinematic diversity suggests expanded roles for fly halteres'
evidence.finding: 'We find a diversity of wing-haltere phase relationships in flight, with higher variability in more ancient families and less in more derived families', and haltere movements during free walking 'were correlated with phylogeny'.

routes.title: Count how often evolution has already deleted wings, and whether it put them back
routes.intervention: None. Read the phylogenetic record of wing loss in stick insects.
routes.predicted_phenotype: THOUSANDS OF INDEPENDENT LOSSES, with about 5% of extant winged-order species flightless, and a contested claim that wings were RE-EVOLVED after loss. For a design space the operational reading is that the wing programme is easy to switch off and is not necessarily destroyed when it is, which is the same point the ant castes make from the network side.
routes.mechanism: Not a mechanism: a phylogenetic pattern. The re-evolution claim depends on the tree and has been argued about since; the page cites the original and does not adjudicate it.

evidence.cite: Whiting MF et al. 2003, Nature 421:264-7, 'Loss and recovery of wings in stick insects'
evidence.finding: 'nearly all pterygote (winged) orders have many partially winged (brachypterous) or wingless (apterous) lineages, and some entire orders are secondarily wingless ... with about 5% of extant pterygote species being flightless. Thousands of independe[nt losses]'.

recommendation.headline: If the question is 'could you redesign an insect's flight apparatus', the honest answer is that it has been done since 1978 and the result flies badly. If the question is 'could you redesign it so that it flies BETTER', the one route nobody has reported trying is the one that fixes what the 1978 result broke: transform the T3 MESODERM as well as the T3 epidermis, so the second pair of wings has an engine. Everything that route needs is published; the combination is not.
why: It is the only route on this page that attacks the actual defect. The four-winged fly's second pair is not a bad wing - Fernandes et al. report it as a wing - it is a wing with 'only rudimentary indirect flight muscles'. Adding an aerofoil without an actuator is the single commonest error in the intuition this page is answering.

Both halves are already published, separately. Roy et al. showed that T2 mesoderm uniquely expresses no bithorax- or Antennapedia-complex selector and is specified entirely by induction, that ectopic homeotic expression IN T2 MESODERM respecifies its muscle, and that Antp persists in transformed-T3 mesoderm. The experiment is to run that in the other direction.
It is scoreable. A thorax either has a second set of indirect flight muscles or it does not, and that is a dissection, not a judgement.

It leaves the page's hard question standing rather than dodging it. Even if the muscle route succeeds, the animal still has no halteres, and our own control model puts the usable feedback-loop delay at about 3 wingbeats - roughly 14 ms - against about 30 ms for vision. So the honest prediction is a four-winged fly that can generate force and cannot hold attitude.
recommendation.the_answer_to_the_judges_question: No - not as posed. Converting halteres into wings costs an actuator AND a sensor to buy a surface, and the published phenotype confirms both costs independently. But 'four wings are worse than two' is NOT a general truth, and the page says so: dragonflies have kept four independently controlled wings for over 300 million years and their fore-hind phasing can IMPROVE efficiency, and moths stripped of their hindwings still fly while losing their evasive manoeuvring. What makes the dipteran case different is that in flies the hindwing has already been spent on something else.
recommendation.what_would_change_our_mind: A measurement of free-flight performance in a four-winged fly. We found none. Every quantitative flight statement on this page about four-winged Drosophila is an inference from the muscle phenotype and from haltere ablation in otherwise normal flies, not a flight measurement in the mutant. That gap is the most important thing on this page and it is stated here rather than buried in the limitations.
recommendation.cheapest_informative_experiment: Load the haltere knob (route sen-haltere-loading). It is reversible, needs no genetics, has a demonstrated recovery control, and separates 'the haltere's MASS matters' from 'the haltere's SENSING matters' - which is the confound in every ablation experiment on this page.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Four wings - and a fly that flies worse, because the transformed segment has only rudimentary indirect flight muscle and the halteres are gone. Not a better flier.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Do they expect the extra pair to be DRIVEN? If yes, they are thinking of the epidermal phenotype and have not met the mesodermal one.

judge_gene_candidates.gene: Ubx, used as a DOSE rather than a switch
judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Intermediate appendages. Wing-like traits appear at about 39% of endogenous Ubx, so the interesting regime is between 100% and 39%, not at zero.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Are they describing a null allele or a knockdown? The two give different organs, and the dose literature is much newer than the allele literature.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: A haltere-LIKE wing, at about 490% of endogenous Antp - the transformation run backwards.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Did the appendage they have in mind gain wing character or lose it?

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: No wing if removed; ECTOPIC WING TISSUE on eyes, legs or antennae if forced. This is the gene to reach for if the ask is 'more wing', as opposed to 'a different wing'.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Do they want an extra wing anywhere, or a second wing in the right place? vg gives the first.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: No wing. Sd is the DNA-binding half of the selector; Vg binding switches which sites it reads.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Are they naming the selector or its co-factor? They are not interchangeable, though the phenotype is similar.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: No wing, by removing the dorsoventral BOUNDARY rather than the wing programme.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Is the phenotype they remember a missing wing or a mis-shapen one? Boundary loss gives the first.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Loss of wing structures with the requirement localised to the HINGE.
Veins in the wrong places or in the wrong number - a venation change, not a wing-number change.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Are they talking about the wing, or about what is drawn ON the wing?

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: Mis-partitioned vein and intervein fates, in a 22-30 hour pupal window - or, at the larval boundary, no wing at all. Same pathway, two completely different phenotypes depending on when you touch it.
Long-winged, flying animals or short-winged, flightless and more fecund ones - a whole-morph switch, on a hormone receptor, with no Hox gene involved.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Do they mean a developmental SWITCH the animal already has, rather than a lesion? Then it is probably this or the aphid polyphenism, not Ubx.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: A wing-LENGTH switch, not a wing-identity switch, and it is expressed in both wing pads - 'different from the canonical model of Ubx expression'.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: Which insect are they thinking of? The same gene name means a different experiment outside Drosophila.

judge_gene_candidates.what_it_would_actually_produce: There isn't one. The haltere is built by Ubx re-reading the wing's own targets at several levels of the hierarchy at once, and the target set changes between stages.
judge_gene_candidates.distinguishing_question: If they say 'the haltere gene', they almost certainly mean Ubx, which is a WING-REPRESSING gene, not a haltere-building one.

welfare.framing: Three of the routes on this page are procedures on living animals that a reviewer will want addressed, and one of them - implanting stimulators into free-flying beetles - is the page's most ethically loaded item precisely because it works. This section is here because the absence of it would be a hole, not as an apology.
welfare.invertebrate_status: Insects are outside the scope of most national animal-research legislation, including EU Directive 2010/63/EU, which covers live non-human vertebrates and cephalopods. That is a statement about the law and NOT an argument that the procedures are ethically free; we did not find, and did not look hard for, a governing framework for insect welfare, and we are not qualified to supply one.
the_three_that_need_it: Haltere ablation and campaniform ablation are irreversible sensory deletions on an animal that then cannot fly freely. The loading route (sen-haltere-loading) achieves a comparable manipulation REVERSIBLY, with a demonstrated recovery, and should be preferred wherever it answers the question.

Implanted stimulators (neu-implanted-stimulator-beetle, neu-honeybee-steering) are surgery followed by imposed behaviour. These are the routes with the clearest dual-use profile on the page, and the page names that rather than leaving it implicit.

Wing clipping and hindwing removal (comp-lepidoptera-hindwing, act-thoracic-linkage) are irreversible and the lepidopteran paper argues explicitly that the loss is lethal in the wild even where it is survivable in a cage.
welfare.refinements_available: The polyphenism routes (org-aphid-polyphenism, org-ant-polyphenism) answer wing-number questions with NO procedure at all - the animal makes both morphs itself. Where a question can be asked there, it should be.
welfare.dual_use: The neurally actuated insect work is funded and published as an engineering programme, and the page presents it as the one route that has already produced a steerable flying animal. We state that plainly because omitting it would misrepresent where the field's capability actually is, and we do not provide operational detail beyond what the cited abstracts state.

limitations: We ran no experiments on any animal. Every route on this page is a reading of someone else's published work, or an explicitly labelled proposal. The three studies are simulations and say so in every caption.

THE CENTRAL GAP, stated in full under `not_claimed`: we found no published measurement of free-flight performance in a four-winged Drosophila, and no free-flight haltere-ablation measurement either. The flat claim 'haltere input is necessary for free flight' appears in this literature as an opening PREMISE - in at least two papers - rather than as a result, and we do not cite it as evidence. So the page's two reasons are not equally well evidenced: the missing flight muscle is direct and quoted; the sensory cost is real but graded, task-dependent and clade-dependent.

Read levels are counted, not claimed. One source was read at full text (Deora, Sane & Sane 2021, via Europe PMC). The rest are abstracts or bare PubMed listings, and every evidence row says which. A row marked `listing` carries an explicit NOT READ note instead of a finding.

We could not reach the full text of the journals that hold most of the quantitative flight literature. The Journal of Experimental Biology returns a bot challenge; Europe PMC has no full text for Fry et al. 2005, Ristroph et al. 2010, Dickerson et al. 2019 or Yarger et al. 2021. That absence was checked with a positive control: the same endpoint returned 164 kB of full text for Deora et al. 2021 (PMC8629423), so the endpoint works and the four absences are real.

Every PMID on this page was resolved against NCBI during this session and every citation string was ASSEMBLED from the record NCBI returned, not typed. The verification run also included a deliberate negative control, PMID 99999999, which resolved to MISSING as it should; a verifier that returns a record for everything is indistinguishable from one that is not running.
One cited source is a PREPRINT and is flagged in its own row: Teoh et al. 2025 on the tp1 steering muscle is a bioRxiv record and has not been peer reviewed.

The page preserves at least three live disagreements rather than reconciling them: whether haltere input is necessary for flight in all flies or only in Calyptratae; whether fore-hind wing interaction helps or hurts, which differs in sign between the dragonfly and the general flapping literature; and whether strepsipteran haltere-like organs are homologous to dipteran halteres at all. Where two sources disagree, both are cited and neither is averaged.

The scale assignment of a route is an editorial choice, not a property of the biology. Several routes act at more than one scale - the Ubx-dally-Dpp route is simultaneously cis-regulatory and a network perturbation - and are filed where they are most useful to a reader, not where they are most correct.

Nothing on this page has been attempted by us. The routes marked `proposed` have, as far as our search found, not been attempted by anyone; that is a statement about what we searched, which was PubMed, and not a survey of the field.

not_claimed.no_free_flight_measurement_of_a_four_win: We found no published measurement of free-flight performance in a four-winged Drosophila. Every quantitative flight statement on this page about that animal is an inference from two separately published phenotypes - rudimentary indirect flight muscle in the transformed segment, and the sensory consequences of losing halteres in otherwise normal flies - plus our own model. Nobody flew one and measured it, as far as our search found.
not_claimed.no_free_flight_haltere_ablation_measurem: The sentence 'haltere input is necessary for free flight' recurs in this literature - we met it in Mureli & Fox 2015 (PMID 26113141) and again in Lea et al. 2026 (PMID 42285096) as 'Halteres are necessary for flight control in all winged flies'. In BOTH it is an opening premise explaining why the experiment is tethered or non-flying, not a result of the paper citing it. We did not find the free-flight ablation measurement it stands on, and we do not cite the premise as evidence.
not_claimed.scope_of_that_negative: PubMed only, searched this session. 'haltere free flight' returns 10 records and 'haltere ablation behaviour flies' returns 7; we read the abstracts of every one that could plausibly carry a free-flight ablation result. A search for the classical primary literature returned nothing: 'Pringle gyroscopic mechanism halteres Diptera' gives 0 records and 'haltere gyroscopic organ equilibrium flies' gives 2, neither of them the 1930s-40s work. MEDLINE's coverage does not reach it, so the absence is a statement about PubMed and NOT about the literature. A positive control on the same queries: 'haltere ablation behaviour flies' does return Dickinson 1999 and Mureli & Fox 2015, so the search runs and discriminates.
not_claimed.what_we_cite_instead: For the sensory cost we cite what was measured: ablation abolishes the equilibrium reflexes in a tethered flight arena (Dickinson 1999); haltere-mediated feedback sets body-saccade amplitude on a magnetic tether while visual feedback does not (Bender & Dickinson 2006); haltereless flies cannot stabilise a wide-field stimulus but fixate figures normally (Mureli & Fox 2015); takeoff velocity and stability fall in Calyptratae and not in other flies (Yarger et al. 2021); and non-flight costs in walking and standing (Daltorio & Fox 2018; Lea et al. 2026).
not_claimed.the_asymmetry_this_creates: The two halves of this page's answer are not equally well evidenced, and that is worth saying rather than smoothing. The missing flight muscle is direct, quoted and unambiguous. The sensory cost is real but graded, task-dependent and clade-dependent. A page that says so is more convincing than one asserting two flat failures.
